detail.abstract: This chapter examines how property portals have brought housing markets into the economy of attention, transforming organisational practices and value chains in the real estate industry. In South Africa, two property platforms have taken control of the market's informational landscape by mediating the housing search process through data extraction and software-asa-service, turning real estate brokers into captive customers. By charging access to their infrastructures, regulating online traffic, and monitoring market interactions, property portals monetize attention, governing the brokerage industry through automated, data-driven pricing mechanisms that transform syndication software and digital neighborhoods into incomeproducing assets. Leveraging their infrastructural power, these platforms have recoded the housing market on their own terms, harnessing the rentier mechanisms of digital capitalism.

title: Computational Presumptions to De-Escalate Data Network Effects and Asymmetries in AI Markets
affiliations: University Villanueva

detail.title: Computational Presumptions to De-Escalate Data Network Effects and Asymmetries in AI Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the enduring interplay between privacy and antitrust in digital and Artificial Intelligence (AI) markets, focusing on the economic characteristics of data network effects and asymmetries. While existing ex ante regulations, such as the Digital Markets Act, attempt to fragment the competitive advantages of dominant platforms by restricting data combinations, these remedies may unduly distort reinforcement learning, essential to AI functionality, and fail to resolve information asymmetries inherent in black-box models.

The analysis, therefore, proposes integrating computational techniques as a regulatory presumption to temper these effects. These tools can effectively minimize the misallocation of resources and enhance privacy. Furthermore, they specifically impede within-user learning, a key driver of data network effects, thereby fostering competition in targeted market segments.

title: Civic Infrastructure as Identity Technology: Modelling Behavioral Returns to Visibility
affiliations: Northumbria University, Northumbria University and Northumbria University

detail.title: Civic Infrastructure as Identity Technology: Modelling Behavioral Returns to Visibility
detail.abstract: Civic infrastructure does more than provide public amenities, it shapes how individuals see one another. This paper develops a behavioral model in which public infrastructure operates as a visibility technology: by increasing the observability of individual contributions to civic life, it alters the reputational returns to prosocial effort. In equilibrium, visibility endogenously sustains civic engagement through recursive expectations, individuals exert effort when they believe others are watching and reciprocating. The model yields testable predictions on monotonicity, heterogeneity, and persistence of civic effort with respect to perceived legibility. Using evidence from the Understanding Society panel, the British Election Study, and the International Values Survey, we test these predictions across settings that differ in informational and institutional transparency. The results confirm the mechanism: greater civic visibility amplifies participation and trust where reputational payoffs are salient, but effects weaken when observability saturates, or reputational shadow prices decline. The findings suggest that investments in civic infrastructure can raise collective effort not merely by lowering costs, but by re-engineering the social optics through which reputations are formed.

title: Conflict between Formal and Informal Ownership in Iranian Law (An Examination of the Conflict between Official Deeds and Contractual Agreements, with Reference to the Supreme Court's Unifying Decisions No. 672 and 673)

detail.title: Conflict between Formal and Informal Ownership in Iranian Law (An Examination of the Conflict between Official Deeds and Contractual Agreements, with Reference to the Supreme Court's Unifying Decisions No. 672 and 673)
detail.abstract: This article examines the conflict between formal and informal ownership (registered deeds and contractual agreements) in Iranian law. Considering the Supreme Court's unifying decisions No. 672 and 673, the legal disputes regarding the validity and effectiveness of these two types of ownership under Iranian law will be analyzed. Furthermore, the consequences of these conflicts on real estate transactions and proposed solutions for mitigating such issues are discussed.

title: Industrial Policy Since the Great Financial Crisis
affiliations: International Institute for Management Development, International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), Global Trade Alert, International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Industrial Policy Since the Great Financial Crisis

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper extends the New Industrial Policy Observatory (NIPO) dataset from 2009 to 2023 by employing large language model techniques to identify policy motivations. We document widespread industrial policy adoption across advanced and emerging market economies since the Great Financial Crisis, which was implemented primarily through subsidies and trade restrictions. We identify a structural break around 2020, characterized by accelerated policy activity and the emergence of “new industrial policies” motivated by supply chain resilience, national security, and geopolitical concerns, in addition to policies focused on competitiveness and climate objectives, which were already prevalent in previous years. Policies have targeted dual-use and various advanced technology sectors, as well as their upstream inputs, such as critical raw materials and minerals. We find that geopolitical risk and tit-for-tat retaliation have played a greater role in driving industrial policy after 2020, and that this support extends beyond existing sectors of comparative advantage.

title: A Tale of Two Forces in the Green Transition: Brown Path Dependency versus Green Expectations
affiliations: Ma Yinchu School of Economics, Tianjin University, City University of Hong Kong (CityU), University of Oxford and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: A Tale of Two Forces in the Green Transition: Brown Path Dependency versus Green Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper analyses the interplay between path dependency and green expectations for green transitions. We use a general equilibrium model with endogenous technological change to highlight that the success of green transitions depends on the expected development of green technologies in the future versus the first-mover advantages of brown technologies accumulated in the past. Without policies, brown path dependence can sustain the advantages of brown technologies in the future. But green transitions are feasible if green expectations can offset this type of dismal path dependence. Policy interventions should offset brown path dependency by enforcing emission caps to restrict the use of brown technologies. The policy mix also benefits from expectations-guided green planning, where green expectations help to direct the future development of green technologies and motivate early transitions towards a path of green innovation. We illustrate our results with patent growth data for China.

title: Public Demand Allocation and Productivity of the Private Sector
affiliations: Università di Bologna and Tübingen University

detail.title: Public Demand Allocation and Productivity of the Private Sector
detail.abstract: We study how variation in the allocation mechanism of public demand shapes firm performance and aggregate productivity. Exploiting the quasi-random implementation of an efficient or lottery-like auction format in the Italian construction sector, we find that when the same amount of public resources is allocated through the efficient mechanism, recipient firms experience about 8% higher revenue growth within three years. The effect is strongest where contracting authorities exhibit greater screening capacity and in less competitive markets. Efficient allocation targets more productive firms, which subsequently secure a larger amount of future public resources. Simulations suggest that replacing lottery-like mechanisms with efficient ones could raise sectoral productivity by about 4%.

title: Model-Free Factor Risk Premia
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Finance Department

detail.title: Model-Free Factor Risk Premia
detail.abstract: I develop a semi-parametric estimator for factor risk premia that is robust to model misspecification. Standard two-pass and GMM estimators produce biased estimates when priced factors are omitted, irrelevant factors are included, or factors are weakly identified. The proposed method avoids these problems by separating the construction of the stochastic discount factor from any factor model specification. The SDF is recovered by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence subject only to no-arbitrage restrictions, and each factor's premium is computed through the marginal moment-R f E[mf ]. This approach ensures that the estimate for any given factor depends only on that factor and the recovered SDF-not on which other factors the researcher specifies. Monte Carlo simulations calibrated to Fama-French-Carhart factors show that the estimator matches conventional methods under correct specification and delivers root mean squared errors 90-99% smaller when priced factors are omitted. Empirically, exponential-tilting estimates for traded factors align closely with timeseries means, while Fama-MacBeth estimates for non-traded macro factors exhibit wild specification sensitivity-with sign reversals and swings exceeding 30 percentage points-that disappear under the robust approach.

title: Metadata as Primary Evidence in Digital Asset Disputes
affiliations: PES University, Faculty of Law, Students

detail.title: Metadata as Primary Evidence in Digital Asset Disputes

detail.abstract: The growth of NFTs, cryptocurrencies, and digital art has created new challenges for proving ownership and authenticity in court. Metadata-the embedded "digital fingerprint" of a file-captures creation, modification, and transfer details, making it crucial for resolving digital asset disputes. In India, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) 2023 recognizes electronic records as primary evidence, but does not clarify how metadata should be authenticated or weighed. This paper examines metadata's evidentiary role under Indian law, focusing on Section 65B certification and key precedents such as Anvar P.V. and Arjun Panditrao. It compares Indian practice with international approaches, notably Hermès v. Rothschild (MetaBirkins), where courts relied on metadata and blockchain records to establish provenance and liability. The study argues for reforms to explicitly recognize metadata, adopt blockchain verification protocols, and align with global best practices, ensuring stronger protection of ownership rights in India's digital economy.

title: A Novel Approach to Hurdle Rate Calibration
affiliations: Qatar Investment Authority, Università del Piemonte Orientale Dipartimento di Studi per l'Economia e l'Impresa and Qatar Investment Authority

detail.title: A Novel Approach to Hurdle Rate Calibration
detail.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a refined framework for quantifying the hurdle rate required for asset inclusion in investment portfolios. An investment is deemed value enhancing if its return-to-risk ratio, adjusted for marginal risk, exceeds the portfolio's current Sharpe ratio, thus improving overall efficiency, rather than diluting it. Our formulation embeds the contextual role of each asset within the portfolio and preserves risk-adjusted performance as measured by the Sharpe ratio. We begin with a CAPM-like representation [12, 5, 3], where the hurdle rate equals the Sharpe ratio of the portfolio times the marginal contribution of the asset to the risk of the portfolio, plus the risk-free rate. However, this conventional specification is largely insensitive to portfolio concentration, as it does not distinguish between systematic and idiosyncratic risk exposures. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a conviction adjusted component [10] that penalizes residual volatility, capturing the potential impact of asset-specific fluctuations on portfolio performance. This component follows a bell-shaped profile, increasing with moderate concentration but diminishing as the asset weight becomes excessive. In highly concentrated cases, we complement it with an idiosyncratic adjustment, ensuring a smooth transition across diversification regimes and a more realistic, weightresponsive hurdle rate. Finally, we extend the framework to a benchmark-relative context, deriving an Active Hurdle Rate that integrates the covariance structure of active returns and incorporates investor tolerance for deviations unexplained by systematic benchmark exposure.

title: Supervising Failing Banks
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Supervising Failing Banks

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of banking supervision in anticipating, monitoring, and disciplining failing banks. We document that supervisors anticipate most bank failures with a high degree of accuracy. Supervisors play an important role in requiring troubled banks to recognize losses, taking enforcement actions, and ultimately closing failing banks. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation in supervisory strictness during the Global Financial Crisis. Stricter supervision leads to more loss recognition, reduced dividend payouts, and an increase in the likelihood and speed of closure. Increased strictness entails a trade-off between a lower resolution cost to the FDIC and reduced credit.

detail.title: Contributions of Artificial Intelligence to Economic Modeling: A Systematic Review

detail.abstract: The aim of this paper is to explore the contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to economic modelling through a systematic review of the literature. The results show that the main artificial intelligence techniques used in economic modelling are machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and multi-agent systems (MAS). The latter can model economic phenomena and behaviour using unstructured data. This means they can analyse large quantities of data, making economic modelling more accurate by reducing cognitive biases and detecting complex, non-linear economic patterns that often escape traditional econometric models with their rigid assumptions. The result is time savings in forecasting and in the production of economic data. AI-based models nevertheless come up against limitations such as the potential biases contained in the training data, which can lead to false results, and a lack of skills and IT resources.

title: Hybrid Methodologies in Software Development with AI: The Role of Business Analysis in Economic Optimization of Personalized Medicine
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: Hybrid Methodologies in Software Development with AI: The Role of Business Analysis in Economic Optimization of Personalized Medicine
detail.abstract: Healthcare digitization is expanding toward a $500 billion market by 2030, highlighting the growing importance of personalized medicine. This paper examines how integrating hybrid software development approaches-such as Scrum with AI algorithms-and business analysis can yield significant economic benefits in this domain. Drawing from a case study based on the NIH Genomic Data Commons, I've observed how this method reduces diagnostic errors by approximately 15% and increases productivity by about 20%. My economic analysis estimates potential global cost savings of roughly $50-100 billion, with the possibility of reaching around $120 billion by 2035 under optimal conditions-though I'll admit these figures feel tentative and need more robust validation. Additionally, it offers faster treatment deployment, reduced infrastructure costs, and enhanced system efficiency. This approach could exert a potentially transformative impact, driving a 30-40% sector growth by 2035 and influencing global economies. I hope this sparks further discussion to refine these ideas.

title: Positive versus Normative Disagreement in Optimal Income Taxation
affiliations: Bocconi University and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Positive versus Normative Disagreement in Optimal Income Taxation
detail.abstract: Optimal income taxes depend on how taxpayers respond to taxation and how society normatively values redistribution. We quantify uncertainty in both components by combining a meta-analysis of 1,205 elasticity estimates of the Elasticity of Taxable Income (ETI) with incentivized experiments with 7,500 U.S. adults making real transfers to households at different income levels. We find that normative disagreement about redistribution explains up to 85% of uncertainty in optimal tax rates, substantially more than positive uncertainty about the ETI. Society values transfers to $20,000-earning households 50 times more than to $100,000-earning households, implying tax rates far above current U.S. policy. Yet, even conservatives' redistributive preferences imply 60% average tax rates for high earners, conflicting with the policies they vote for. We show that this is explained by government aversion: many people have strong redistributive preferences but aversion to governmentmediated redistribution impedes support for progressive taxation. Our findings demonstrate that uncertainty over optimal income taxes stems primarily from normative disagreement about redistribution and the role of government, rather than from behavioral responses to taxes.

detail.abstract: The cost of prescription drugs to U.S. health plans depends on a nominal "list" price and a hidden rebate. Using a model of health insurance design, we show that when plans must provide a minimum level of coverage, sponsors have an incentive to use list prices to circumvent coverage restrictions and increase patient cost-sharing. Using exposure to the Medicaid market as an instrument, we confirm that higher list prices lead to higher patient out-of-pocket costs. Consistent with the model, pass-through rates are lowest for PPO and HMO commercial plans and highest for more constrained HDHP and Medicare Part D plans.

title: The Untapped Potential of Microfinance in Bridging Climate Finance Gaps for Smallholder Farmers in Developing Economies: A Case Study of Sub-Saharan Africa in the Era of Net-Zero Transitions
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Untapped Potential of Microfinance in Bridging Climate Finance Gaps for Smallholder Farmers in Developing Economies: A Case Study of Sub-Saharan Africa in the Era of Net-Zero Transitions
detail.abstract: This study examines the critical but underexplored role of microfinance institutions (MFIs) in addressing the massive climate finance gaps facing smallholder farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa. Despite representing 80% of food production in the region, smallholder farmers receive only 1.7% of tracked climate finance. Our mixedmethods analysis reveals that climate-adaptive microfinance products can reduce default rates by 25-40% compared to traditional lending, while enabling farmers to invest in climate-resilient technologies. Through case studies of innovative programs in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, we demonstrate how mobile money-enabled microfinance platforms are scaling climate finance delivery from $10 million to over $100 million annually. We introduce the Climate-Adaptive Microfinance Index (CAMI) as a novel framework for measuring institutional readiness to bridge climate finance gaps. Our findings indicate that strategic integration of microfinance with blended finance mechanisms could unlock $25-30 billion in additional climate finance for smallholder farmers by 2030, contributing significantly to net-zero agricultural transitions while advancing SDGs 1, 2, and 13.

title: Soft information in mutual fund portfolios
affiliations: Department of Finance, University of Central Florida , University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance, Tsinghua University and University of Central Florida - College of Business Administration

detail.title: Soft information in mutual fund portfolios
detail.abstract: We identify soft information acquisition by mutual fund managers based on detailed data on investor company visits in China and study the use of soft information in portfolio management. We find a clear divergence in fund managers’ preference for soft information in investment decisions. “Soft-information” managers hold fewer stocks and tend to invest in companies with high growth potential and significant idiosyncratic risk. Trades driven by soft information acquisition are profitable, resulting in superior performance by these managers, especially in their holdings of stocks rich with soft information. Fund managers’ distinct preferences for soft versus hard information create segmentation in both information acquisition and portfolio choice. ​

detail.title: Labor Markets, Migration, and EU Integration in the Western Balkans

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural model of interconnected European labor markets to examine how further EU integration would impact the Western Balkan economies and how policy can improve output and employment in these countries. Risks of increased emigration from further integration can be managed through promoting faster productivity growth, including through structural reforms. Model simulations show that productivity increases of 30 percent, similar to previous EU accession cases, would results in wage growth, help close the unemployment gap, and offset increased emigration through higher immigration and labor participation. Policies to improve the efficiency of the labor market (participation, job search, production) are essential to boost employment and support output.

title: Maximum Sustainable Debt Across Countries

detail.title: Maximum Sustainable Debt Across Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides a parsimonious yet tractable approach to evaluating maximum sustainable debt across countries and over time within the p-theory framework developed by Jiang et al. (2024). By incorporating tax distortions, asset-pricing components (risk-free rates, convenience yields, and jump-risk premia), and sovereign default risks into the model, we calibrate it for a large sample of over 170 countries. Our illustrative findings show that while current debt levels in many economies remain within maximum sustainable debt levels, debt burdens in many emerging markets and low-income countries are near their respective sustainable levels. In contrast, a few countries that are in—or at high risk of—debt distress have debt levels exceeding their sustainable thresholds. The analysis highlights how sustainable debt estimates evolve over time in response to shifts in financial conditions and macro-fiscal fundamentals. These estimates are particularly sensitive to key parameters—most notably when interest-growth differentials are narrow.

title: A Quantitative Approach to Central Bank Haircuts and Counterparty Risk Management

detail.title: A Quantitative Approach to Central Bank Haircuts and Counterparty Risk Management

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for determining haircuts on collateral used in central bank operations, quantifying residual uncollateralized exposures, and validating haircut models using machine learning. First, it introduces four haircut model types tailored to asset characteristics—marketable or non-marketable—and data availability. It proposes a novel model for setting haircuts in data-limited environment using a satallite cross-country model. Key principles guiding haircut calibration include non-procyclicality, data-drivenness, conservatism, and the avoidance of arbitrage gaps. The paper details model inputs such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) percentiles, volatility measures, and time to liquidation. Second, it proposes a quantitative framework for estimating expected uncollateralized exposures that remain after haircut application, emphasizing their importance in stress scenarios. Illustrative simulations using dynamic Nelson-Siegel yield curve models demonstrate how volatility impacts exposure. Third, the paper explores the use of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to simulate stress scenarios for bond yields. Trained on U.S. Treasury data, VAEs capture realistic yield curve distributions, offering an altenative tool for validating VaR-based haircuts. Although interpretability and explainability remain concerns, machine learning models enhance risk assessment by uncovering potential model vulnerabilities.

detail.abstract: Older home sellers receive lower returns than younger home sellers. Homes sold by older people have fewer major renovations but higher rates of poor upkeep. Older sellers are also more likely to sell off-MLS (“pocket listings”) and to sell to investors, leading to lower prices. These patterns suggest that older sellers may be disproportionately disadvantaged by agents’ incentive to maximize fees through generating high sales volume instead of maximizing sale prices. Age-related cognitive decline makes the elderly more vulnerable. For causal evidence, we show that reforms making private listings more transparent reduced both the prevalence of pocket listings and the magnitude of the age gap in returns.

detail.abstract: Gauging the Experience of Latin American Journalists with Access to Information Laws Over the past three decades, close to 140 countries worldwide-including 18 in Latin America-have enacted access to information laws (ATI). Recent increases in populism, authoritarianism, and harassment of the press, however, have been accompanied by rollbacks in public transparency and ATI, raising questions about the factors shaping journalists' use and perceptions of ATI laws and government transparency more generally. In one of the largest cross-national ATI surveys to date, we draw on responses from 678 journalists across Latin America to examine the influence of macro-level factors-including populist leadership, press freedom, and characteristics of ATI laws-on journalists' experiences with information access. Our findings show that populist leadership has significantly negative effects on ATI use and experience, in line with other evaluations. However, our findings reveal several unexpected results, including the null effect of the age and legal strength of ATI laws on usage and the statistically significant relationship between negative press freedom and increased ATI use. Overall, our results show that two-thirds of our sample make use of information access laws. And despite negative experiences, journalists continue to file information requests, and the more requests they file, the more positive their assessment of government transparency. Our study thus suggests that ATI laws provide substantially positive returns to both journalists and governments.

detail.abstract: Amid rising international tensions, notably the ongoing Russia-Ukraine and Hamas-Israel conflicts, countries around the world are reassessing their defense budgets with seriousness not        seen since the Cold War. This paper investigates empirically whether national defense budgets align with actual security needs and underlying economic fundamentals. Using the framework of        Borcherding and Deacon (1972) and Bergstrom and Goodman (1973), we estimate the determinants of national defense spending for a longitudinal panel of 150 countries from 1950 to 2016. Our        findings reveal that national defense expenditures exhibit a high degree of rivalry, often being closer to 1 than 0 on the Samuelson Index. Our results call for a critical reassessment of defense        allocation strategies and optimization of public resource management. detail.title: From Servers to Rates

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the macroeconomic implications of the rising wave of investment in information and communication technology (ICT)—including AI-related hardware and software—in the U.S. economy. The analysis uses a structural macroeconomic model that treats ICT as a distinct type of capital and explores the degree to which ICT complements or substitutes for labor. The findings reveal three key insights. First, labor and ICT have historically been only moderately substitutable. Second, technological innovations that make it easier to turn ICT investment into productive capital act like demand shocks, boosting output and inflation. Third, given the uncertainty surrounding the interaction between AI-driven ICT capital and labor, the paper presents scenarios of possible trajectories for ICT investment under alternative assumptions. When ICT tends to complement labor, the economy experiences strong gains in output, but also inflationary pressure; the natural interest rate increases, requiring tighter monetary policy. Conversely, if ICT tends to replace labor, the same ICT investment path warrants a looser monetary policy stance.

detail.abstract:
This article analyses the likely impact of the collaborative activity exception to the prohibition in the New Zealand Commerce Act on cartel conduct. Cartel provisions are provisions in arrangements between competitors which have the purpose, effect or likely effect of price fixing, restricting output or market allocating.

The collaborative activity exception applies where the parties are participants in a collaborative venture that does not have the dominant purpose of lessening competition between the parties, and the cartel provision is reasonably necessary for the purpose of the collaborative activity.

The article discusses a number of different forms of business collaborations including production or marketing collaborations, research and development collaborations and collaborative business models such as open payment systems.

The article concludes that the application of the collaborative activity exception to particular collaborations will require factual analysis that can be guided by economic principles.

One key question is whether there are likely to be sufficiently large efficiency enhancing effects from a collaboration so that a dominant purpose may be inferred which is not the lessening of competition. Another key question is whether any cartel provisions are necessary to generate the incentives and conditions required for successful collaboration, or whether less restrictive arrangements could achieve a similar outcome.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between internet access and Native American economic development. First, it synthesizes various insights from institutional economics and        market-process economics to examine how expanded internet access can improve development on reservations. Reliable, high-speed internet access facilitates a greater degree of specialization        and exchange, contributing to economic growth for Native American communities. Internet access directly contributes to development because it provides more ways for private entrepreneurs and        tribally owned enterprises to reach consumers, as well as outside firms to exchange with reservation residents. Reliable, high-speed internet access indirectly aids economic development by        improving human capital through better access to education and telemedicine. Technological innovations and institutional reforms can reduce the costs of providing internet. Second, this paper        describes the real-world institutional and economic barriers that limit internet access on reservations. Third, this paper uses a case study of the Colville Indian Reservation to examine how        a real-world technological innovation has improved internet access, thus expanding the extent of the market and facilitating development. The case study is instructive because it examines how        recent technological innovations on the Colville Indian Reservation have augmented opportunities in business, health, and education. Keywords: economic development, Native American, internet,        telecommunications, innovation, entrepreneurship, institutions, market access

affiliations: GIGA - Hamburg, Institute of African Affairs

detail.title: Africa's Demographic Dividend or Demographic Disaster? A Continent at a Crossroads
detail.abstract: As the world’s youngest region, Africa has the potential to reap a significant demographic dividend, which could boost economic growth, drive innovation, and reshape global labour markets. As the continent progresses through its demographic transition, changes in age distribution, workforce composition and dependency ratios will have wide-reaching consequences for economic growth, social services and development planning. While demographic trends offer an unprecedented opportunity, policy and governance will ultimately determine whether this potential is realised. Supporting Africa’s demographic journey is not only a matter of global equity, but also in the interest of achieving long-term stability and prosperity. In Africa, the proportion of the working-age population to the total population is still growing and will peak shortly after 2070. However, Africa’s peak worker-to-dependent ratio will be low, which translates into relatively modest potential for rapid economic growth. With few exceptions, average economic growth rates in Africa are too slow and population growth rates too high to enable the continent to rapidly reduce poverty or raise average incomes. Although fertility rates and dependency ratios in Africa remain high, they have begun to decline. According to UN projections, these rates will continue to fall in the coming decades, meaning that by the mid-21st century, the ratio of the working-age population to the dependent population will be higher than in Asia, Europe and North America. Africa has considerable potential to benefit from a demographic dividend. Whether, when and to what extent this occurs hinges on policies and institutions in key areas such as macroeconomic management, human capital, trade, governance, and labour and capital markets. If African countries can continue to build on their hard-won development gains, the demographic dividend could account for 11–15% of gross domestic product (GDP) growth by 2030, reducing the number of people living in poverty by 40–60 million. The continent is set to become a population superpower. Its proportion of the world's population is increasing in an unprecedented manner, especially relative to Europe, and its inhabitants are younger than ever. The youth bulge heading Africa's way is real and, in the next 30 years, it will present African states with economic, social, and political problems the likes of which the world has never witnessed before. This demographic surge is neither a catastrophe nor a boon; it is a wicked problem. -

keywords: Balanced Growth Path Vs. Accelerating Growth Path

contentType.other: The paper is being considered by a journal but not yet accepted for publication

detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to introduce a new production function that takes into account selflearning AI, which can improve itself and therefore productivity without any additional human capital or labor, even though it still requires physical capital. The difference between my production function and any other existing production function is that my production function separates technologies into self-learning and non-self-learning technologies. The value of exponent for the self-learning technologies depends on the value of its base and this is the unique recursive feature of my production function. Unlike in the Mankiw-Romer-Weil production function, in my production function, technology and labor force are separated and this is allowed because I make the technology endogenous. My production function leads to only two possibilities, which are an economy that is in balanced growth path (BGP), and an economy that is in accelerating growth path. The determining factor that decides whether an economy is in BGP or not is the exponent for the self-learning technologies in my production function. If the sum of all exponents is less or equal to 1, then the economy is in BGP, which is consistent with Mankiw-Romer-Weil (1992). If the sum of all exponents is greater than 1, then the economy is in accelerating growth path, which is consistent with Romer (1986). There is no steady state in my production function. I also rule out the possibility of singularity. My production function has many policy implications, which differ among AI-producing, rich non-AI-producing and poor non-AIproducing countries.

detail.abstract: Commentators on Adam Smith’s Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations often characterize Smith as a proponent of government in multiple areas, including security in        person, property, contract, and some public goods. However, Smith understood government more expansively than people today. In volume I, book III, chapters I–IV, Smith describes the evolution        of merchant towns in England that led to “good governance” that dismantled the feudal system. This limited government not only included the security provided by the formal laws and        institutions. It also aligned the informal elements of individual civic ethics and self- reliance with the formal institutions. This Smithian combination of formal and informal government        encouraged liberty and market exchange, which enriched towns and, then, agriculture. It established the foundation for English economic development, which made the nation wealthy.

detail.abstract: How has the European Union transformed its policy arsenal to counter coercion? This work introduces geo-legality—a condition wherein legal-normative authority counters external coercion—examining how the EU has redefined its self-defense amid contemporary rivalry between great powers (such as itself and China). Analyzing China’s 2021–2022 economic coercion against Lithuania, following Lithuania’s acceptance of a “Taiwanese Representative Office,” I demonstrate how targeted pressure catalyzed Brussels’ institutional innovation, including the Anti-Coercion Instrument, WTO litigation (DS-610), enhanced investment screening, and reforms to the Blocking Statute. Through process tracing, comparative jurisprudential analysis, and Delphi consultation with 23 EU institutional actors, the present work reveals how the EU as a mid-sized power may neutralize material coercion by institutionalizing legal counter-leverage and using regulatory precedents to lock in procedural advantages. Ultimately, the findings show that regulatory rule-setting has become the core terrain for contesting (geo-)strategic agency in contemporary global affairs and governance.

detail.abstract: Superficial consideration of market fundamentals has permitted prominent critics of private enterprise from John Kenneth Galbraith to 2017 Nobelist Richard Thaler to maintain that premia        on closed-ended funds (that is, investment trusts) prior to the stock market crash of 1929 are prima facie evidence of investor irrationality. We provide the first-ever fundamentals- focused        inquiry into the pricing of investment trusts that year. Applying multiple empirical methods to a large sample of about three thousand observations, we assess the pricing and fundamentals of        two informationally polar types of trusts: transparent trusts whose portfolios were published throughout the year; and blind trusts whose portfolios were unpublished until the third-quarter        reporting week. Consistent with the efficient market hypothesis, when new information about blind trusts hit the market, their prices quickly corrected. This was the great correction of        1929.

detail.abstract: Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding during a period of grid congestion, volatile peak prices, and uneven water availability. As AI data centers draw increasing electricity, the associated costs and externalities—capacity additions, transmission upgrades, marginal emissions, and water withdrawals—risk concentrating in disadvantaged communities already facing higher energy burdens and proximity to polluting assets.[EPA_EJScreen_2024][DOE_LEAD] Objective. We evaluate where incremental data-center training and inference load may impose public costs and propose a measurable, auditable remedy: a Self-Powered AI Standard. Methods. We define four core metrics: (i) Attributable Additional Clean Share (AACS), the fraction of consumption served by new, attributable clean generation; (ii) 24/7 Clean Match Rate, the share of site-hours (and an energy-weighted variant) matched to clean supply within the relevant balancing area or bidding zone; (iii) Firm Self-Supply Availability (FSSA), the share of hours the site can operate at rated IT load without imports given reserve and black-start requirements; and (iv) Scarcity-Adjusted Import Exposure (SAIE), a penalty for importing during price/CO₂ scarcity hours. We also report LCAP (Levelized Cost of AI Power) for self-supplied stacks, with sensitivity analyses grounded in standards and public datasets.[ASHRAE_2021_Thermal] Data. Using public indicators of scarcity—peak and capacity prices, interconnection queues, marginal emissions, transmission congestion, and water stress—we construct a screening map of harm exposure and synthesize efficiency levers across product/workload, facility, and grid layers. Water context draws on national accounts.[USGS_Water_Use_2023] Results. Scarcity hot spots align with areas of higher energy burden; efficiency levers materially reduce kWh per useful outcome; and self-powered architectures can avoid the most harmful hours while supporting new clean build. Governance mechanisms—24/7 hourly matching across portfolios, demand-response enrollment, and import caps—enable operator balancing without leaning on the public during scarcity windows.[FERC_2222] Conclusions. Treating AI as a load—and requiring deployments to supply, match, and firm their own energy— offers a practical path to protect vulnerable communities while allowing compute to scale. Intergovernmental and federal analyses indicate data-center electricity demand is set to more than double this decade, underscoring the urgency of auditable standards.[IEA_2025_AI_DC][LBNL_2024_DC_Report]

title: Sovereignty as a Priced Asset: Brexit and the UK's Fiscal Capacity
affiliations: Northwestern University, Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: Sovereignty as a Priced Asset: Brexit and the UK's Fiscal Capacity
detail.abstract: This paper develops a positive theory of the financial consequences of political sovereignty, using the United Kingdom as a natural experiment. The 2016 Brexit referendum is modelled as a sovereignty shock—a fall in the country’s fiscal and financial integration with the European core—while the 2022 “Truss mini-budget’’ represents a fiscal shock under reduced integration. In a continuous-time international asset-pricing model with incomplete risk sharing and an endogenous fiscal constraint, lower integration tightens fiscal capacity, raises gilt risk premia, and reduces their convenience yield as safe assets. These channels widen the gilt–Bund spread, increase the EUR/GBP currency risk premium, and depreciate sterling through a modified uncovered-interest-parity condition. Calibrated to event-study data, the model reproduces the observed 10–15 bp rise in spreads, 40 bp increase in currency risk premia, 6–10 percent pound depreciation after Brexit, and the 2022 gilt yield spike. The results quantify the financial price of sovereignty: autonomy amplifies market discipline but reduces fiscal space.

title: The Evolution of Portfolio Theory: Integrating Machine Learning with Markowitz Optimization
affiliations: University of Edinburgh

detail.title: The Evolution of Portfolio Theory: Integrating Machine Learning with Markowitz Optimization
detail.abstract: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), developed by Harry Markowitz, transformed investment practices by wisely balancing risk and return. Nonetheless, its efficacy wanes in fluctuating financial markets due to its dependence on historical data and fixed assumptions. This paper investigates incorporating Machine Learning (ML) techniques into the traditional Markowitz optimization framework to enhance portfolio construction and risk management processes. It highlights the use of supervised learning for forecasting asset returns, unsupervised learning for asset clustering, and reinforcement learning for adjusting portfolios dynamically. An empirical analysis utilizing recent U.S. market data reveals that ML models improve risk assessment, asset selection, and adaptive portfolio allocation. Techniques such as linear regression, clustering algorithms, and principal component analysis (PCA) facilitate superior forecasting and portfolio design in various market environments. The research also shows that ML can enhance Sharpe ratios in specific market conditions compared to conventional MPT. ML increases portfolio flexibility and robustness by aligning predictive modeling with optimization objectives. This evolving methodology lays the foundation for a more responsive, data-informed investment strategy in today's finance, providing a viable alternative to the limitations of traditional models.

detail.title: Do Capital Requirements and Their International Differences Affect Banks' Profitability?

publicationDetails.journalName: Deutsche Bundesbank Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: A key element of the Basel III reforms are stricter capital requirements, which have been implemented with varying degrees of stringency across jurisdictions. We examine the impact of these requirements on bank profitability in the US and Europe between 2019 and 2024. We find no evidence that higher capital ratios or requirements negatively affect profitability. However, our results indicate that international differences in capital requirements can influence the profitability of banks that operate globally: Since capital requirements in a jurisdiction apply only to domestic banks and foreign subsidiaries, foreign banks operating through cross-border or branch-based activities may gain a competitive advantage. Nevertheless, the effect appears to be limited to the subsample of German significant institutions (SIs). Moreover, our analysis of policy scenarios based on the estimated spillover effects suggests that lowering capital requirements is not an effective strategy for improving bank profitability and could even be detrimental if reciprocated by foreign jurisdictions.

detail.title: The Decline of Congregate Care in the United States Foster Care System, 2004-2022
detail.abstract: BackgroundThe use of congregate care (CC) has declined substantially in the US in the past 20 years. The Family First Prevention Services Act of 2018 (FFPSA), which sought to curb the use of CC, is often understood to be a central driver in this decline. However, much of the decline occurred in the years preceding FFPSA. The nature of the decline in the years preceding and following FFPSA remains unknown.ObjectivesTo understand how states reduced CC from 136,000 placements in 2004 to 39,000 placements in 2022.Participants and SettingAll children in out-of-home care in 2004, 2018, and 2022 in the US.MethodsThis study uses federal foster care census files and decomposition analysis to examine national and state-specific changes in CC placements before and after FFPSA, which limited federal cost sharing for CC placements. We decompose the difference in CC placements between 2004 and 2018 (pre-FFPSA) and the difference between 2018 and 2022 (post-FFPSA).ResultsCC placements declined by 69,411 between 2004 and 2018, driven by reduced shares of older, behaviorally-complex children in the foster care system and reduced use of CC for younger, lower-needs children. CC placements declined by 28,077 between 2018 and 2022, overwhelmingly due to decreases in the foster care population size rather than reduced use of CC within foster care.ConclusionsStates’ capacity to maintain older and behaviorally-complex children into kinship or other family foster care remains limited following FFPSA; rather, those children are less likely to enter foster care at all.

title: Geopolitics and Innovation: A Systematic Literature Review of Firm Responses to the U.S.-China Trade War

detail.title: Geopolitics and Innovation: A Systematic Literature Review of Firm Responses to the U.S.-China Trade War
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study aims to systematically examine how the U.S.-China trade war has shaped firm-level innovation activities. It identifies key risk factors triggered by geopolitical tensions, analyzes firm-level responses, and evaluates long-term strategic shifts in innovation and industrial strategies.

Methodology: The study employed a systematic literature review (SLR) approach following established guidelines for transparent and replicable synthesis. A structured search across ScienceDirect, JSTOR, and Emerald databases was conducted using Boolean keyword combinations related to the trade war and innovation. A total of sixteen empirical studies were identified and analyzed descriptively, focusing on theoretical mechanisms, empirical findings, and contextual variations. Findings: The review finds that the trade war introduced substantial trade policy uncertainty (TPU), producing heterogeneous impacts across firms and sectors. Financially constrained and export-dependent firms reduced R&D and experienced declines in patent quality, while larger firms and those with state support increased innovation. Common adaptive responses included geographic diversification of R&D, ESG-driven innovation, and the pursuit of indigenous technologies. TPU thus functions not only as a constraint but also as a conditional driver of "precautionary innovation" aimed at reducing foreign dependence and securing long-term competitiveness.

Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: This study provides one of the first systematic syntheses of firm-level innovation responses to the U.S.-China trade war. It contributes to theory by framing trade policy uncertainty as both a deterrent and a stimulus to innovation. For policymakers, it highlights the importance of coordinated industrial policies that enhance resilience and technological self-reliance. For practitioners, it offers insights into how firms can transform external shocks into opportunities for long-term strategic adaptation and innovation-led competitiveness.

title: Lithium’s “resource curse”: aquatic environment risks from the Chinese clean energy industry

detail.title: Lithium’s “resource curse”: aquatic environment risks from the Chinese clean energy industry
detail.abstract: Rapidly increasing lithium-ion battery production, central to transitioning to clean energy, is increasing anthropogenic lithium emissions to aquatic environments. China supplies 77% of global lithium-ion battery capacity but lacks national monitoring of lithium in water and faces environmental risks. We determined lithium in water samples from around China and reached three conclusions. (1) Lithium concentrations in tap water strongly spatially vary. Concentrations were higher in western cities than eastern cities (p=0.0096) because of geological sources (e.g., salt lakes) and mining. The lithium concentration in tap water from Lhasa was 77.8 µg L−1, 7.8 times the US Environmental Protection Agency reference concentration. (2) The mean and median lithium concentrations in Yangtze River water were 29.4% and 34.0% higher, respectively, in 2025 than 2006 and were higher downstream than upstream of mining hubs. (3) Wastewater treatments gives very low lithium removal efficiencies (<16% for anaerobic–oxic and anaerobic–anoxic–oxic processes), meaning lithium accumulates in aquatic environments. These results indicate a triple paradox – resource abundance/ecological vulnerability, industry growth/inadequate pollution control, and emerging health risks/regulatory gaps – that require urgent lifecycle governance strategies to align lithium utilization with UN Sustainable Development Goals 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).

title: Increasing price transparency in the Dutch healthcare market does not affect provider choice
affiliations: Tilburg University, Tilburg University - Department of Econometrics & Operations Research, University of Twente and Tilburg University

detail.title: Increasing price transparency in the Dutch healthcare market does not affect provider choice
detail.abstract: AbstractPrice transparency is often viewed as an effective way to encourage price shopping and thereby lower healthcare expenditure. We use individual claims data to estimate the short-run effect of unexpected publication of prices by a major Dutch health insurer on spending and provider choice. The media reported prominently on potential savings and visits to websites providing information on prices initially increased. Another major insurer had negotiated different prices and did not publish them, so its patients serve as the control group in a difference-in-differences analysis. We first perform a case study of 6 frequent, non-emergency dermatological procedures. We find that spending, the likelihood to visit a new provider, and the distance traveled to the chosen provider remained unaffected. Next, we analyze a broader set of 675 procedures. We estimate the effect for each procedure and then perform a Bayesian meta-analysis to summarize the results. Again, we find that there is no effect of price transparency on spending. We provide an explanation for this and make a suggestion for a policy change that would make it more likely that patients choose cheaper providers.

title: Machine Learning-Based Lead Prioritization to Enhance B2C Sales Efficiency

detail.title: Machine Learning-Based Lead Prioritization to Enhance B2C Sales Efficiency
detail.abstract: This paper presents a machine learning-driven approach to lead prioritization that replaces the traditional first-come, first-serve (FCFS) system in customer relationship management (CRM). The proposed system predicts conversion probabilities for incoming leads and dynamically assigns priority levels, ensuring that high-potential leads are addressed first. Using a production-scale dataset of more than 380,000 records, the XGBoost model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.9158, PR-AUC of 0.3604, accuracy of 0.9241, precision of 0.315 and F1 score of 0.3919. The results confirm that the model outperforms heuristic FCFS allocation by identifying promising leads early in the pipeline. We detail the methodology, deployment architecture, and evaluation metrics, providing a replicable framework for intelligent CRM automation.

title: Trade Secret Law in the United States: Evolution, Framework, and Federalization
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: Trade Secret Law in the United States: Evolution, Framework, and Federalization

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper traces the evolution of trade secret law in the United States from its origins in fragmented state common law to its current dual-track framework under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA) and the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA). It explains how the drive for predictability in a nationalized, information-driven economy led to codification of doctrines once rooted in tort, contract, and equity. The UTSA brought coherence by unifying definitions of “trade secret” and “misappropriation,” yet preserved flexibility through its state-based adoption model—creating what the paper terms a “uniformity paradox.” The DTSA further transformed the field by introducing a federal civil cause of action, aligning trade secrets with other federally recognized IP rights while deliberately avoiding preemption of state law. The analysis explores the continuing divergence among states in key areas such as the inevitable disclosure doctrine and employee mobility, illustrating how American federalism sustains diversity within a largely harmonized system. The paper concludes that U.S. trade secret law today is unified but not uniform: a pragmatic equilibrium between consistency and experimentation that reflects enduring policy tensions between innovation, competition, and labor freedom in the knowledge economy.

title: The Trust Stack: How We Rebuild Credibility Online
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: The Trust Stack: How We Rebuild Credibility Online

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The internet was never designed with a native layer of trust. As deepfakes, AI-generated misinformation, and engagement-driven algorithms flood the information ecosystem, traditional cues of authenticity have collapsed. This paper argues that rebuilding credibility online requires a systemic response—a “trust stack” that reintroduces verifiable provenance and semantic assessment into digital infrastructure. Drawing on behavioral science and design principles, it outlines how machine-readable trust indicators, modeled on security standards like HTTPS, could allow users to assess authenticity at a glance. The first layer would certify provenance through cryptographic metadata, as in emerging initiatives like the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). A second, semantic layer would use AI and knowledge graphs to evaluate factual consistency and sourcing, translating complex verification into intuitive user signals. The paper compares this approach to labeling systems such as Nutri-Score and Creative Commons, identifying both their behavioral power and their vulnerability to industry capture. It concludes that trust must become an opt-out default of the digital ecosystem, driven by open standards, independent governance, and interoperable “trust-as-a-service” tools. The internet’s integrity, it suggests, depends not on censorship but on transparency engineered into its very code.

detail.abstract: Nursing home costs in the United States now exceed $100,000 per year, and government assistance programs such as Medicaid help out only when retirees are largely destitute. Moreover, health shocks driving the need for such care can arise suddenly in old age, are frequently permanent in nature, and can be associated with declining mental and physical abilities. These facts raise the important question of how households can best prepare to finance this final phase of life. Building on past research, we determine how retirees should manage payouts from defined contribution plans to balance trade-offs between consumption and health care cost shocks, using both retirement plan assets and annuitization. Our analysis explicitly integrates the role of taxes, required minimum distributions, bequest motives, and the possibility of retiree insolvency. We conclude that payout annuities, especially deferred and variable annuities, can be quite valuable for retirees, even when they face health shocks in later life.

title: Sugar supplementation affects ant-mealybug mutualism and promote natural enemies for mealybug control in pineapple systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sugar supplementation affects ant-mealybug mutualism and promote natural enemies for mealybug control in pineapple systems
detail.abstract: Honeydew-producing hemipterans establish mutualistic interactions with ants, which collect honeydew while providing protection against natural enemies and other services. Although this association benefits hemipterans, it often exacerbates crop damage by increasing pest abundance. Providing alternative sugar resources has been proposed as a strategy to disrupt these associations, but its effectiveness remains poorly tested in tropical agrosystems. Here, we investigated whether sugar feeders could reduce ant-mealybug interactions in pineapple (Ananas comosus) fields on La Réunion, where the mealybug Dysmicoccus brevipes, a vector of Pineapple Mealybug Wilt-associated viruses (PMWaVs), poses a major threat to production. We deployed sugar feeders in replicated field plots and monitored ant, mealybug and predator abundances over ten months, complemented by sentinel prey assays to assess ant aggressiveness toward mealybugs. Mealybug abundance was positively associated with ant presence, while sugar supplementation reduced ant abundance by 42% on pineapple plants compared to controls. Predator abundance was higher in supplemented zones, likely due to both direct nutritional benefits and lower ant interference, but declined with distance from feeders. Three ant species, Solenopsis geminata, Pheidole megacephala and Brachymyrmex cordemoyi accounted for most interactions with mealybugs, with species-specific temporal dynamics but no response to sugar supplementation. Sugar supplementation represents a promising management lever, but its effect on mealybug remains context-dependent. Integrating sugar provisioning with complementary agroecological practices, such as biological control and habitat diversification, may maximize its impact and contribute to sustainable management of pineapple mealybug wilt disease.

title: Optional Fee-Shifting
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis, University of Bern - Institute of Economics and University of St.Gallen

detail.title: Optional Fee-Shifting

publicationDetails.journalName: University of Minnesota Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study settlement bargaining under three alternative fee-shifting rules: the American Rule, the English Rule, and an optional fee shifting regime in which the defendant chooses whether the case will proceed under the American or the English Rule. The defendant knows whether his conduct gives rise to liability while the plaintiff only has a noisy signal. This two-sided asymmetric information creates scope for strategic misrepresentation: defendants who face liability may try to pass as if they do not, while plaintiffs with weak evidence may act as if they have a strong case. Optional fee-shifting has an information-generating function which, however, can be distorted by strategic efforts to send misleading signals. When litigation costs are similar for both parties, optional fee-shifting reduces litigation rates more effectively than either the American or the English Rule alone.

title: Seeking Advice from Doctor's Doctor? The Impact of Physician Peer Recognition on Patient Choice
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology and Texas Tech University - Area of Information Systems and Quantitative Sciences (ISQS)

detail.title: Seeking Advice from Doctor's Doctor? The Impact of Physician Peer Recognition on Patient Choice

declarations.ethicsApproval: All our data was collected from a large online healthcare webite that provides API for public use. All the data is publicly available for access and collection. In the data, there is no identifiable personal information or other personal information of patients or physicians. We did not do any survey or experiments, so there were no individual participants in our study.

detail.abstract: On online healthcare platforms (OHPs), a critical operational challenge pertains to helping patients find suitable physicians amid significant information asymmetries between the two parties. While patient-generated reviews are common, their utility is often limited due to patients' lack of medical knowledge and expertise. To address this issue, some OHPs have introduced physician peer recognition, where peer physicians provide expert endorsements for focal (recognized) physicians to guide patient choices. However, it is not clear whether and how physicians' peer recognition may affect patients' selection of physicians and participation in physicians' online consultations. We fill this gap by empirically examining the effect of physicians' peer recognition on focal physicians' consultation volume, along with its underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions. Using a large-scale dataset from a leading OHP, we find that physicians' peer recognition significantly increases patients' participation in focal physicians' online consultations. Our mechanism analysis suggests that this effect is driven by specific characteristics of the recognition content, particularly its types (e.g., ability-based and attitude-based recognition) and language attributes (e.g., certainty, length, and positive sentiment). However, the positive impact of physicians' peer recognition is weakened when the recognition is reciprocal, as it may raise patients' skepticism about the objectivity of the recognition. Furthermore, we find that physicians' peer recognition and patient evaluations act as complements, synergistically exerting a positive influence on patient consultation decisions. Our study contributes to the literature on operations management on OHPs, peer recognition, and patient consultation decision-making, offering practical implications for the service operations of OHPs.

title: Applying HRNS and Fuzzy MCDM to Map Risks in Rope Access Work
affiliations: Istanbul Yeni Yüzyıl University and Istanbul Yeni Yüzyıl University

detail.title: Applying HRNS and Fuzzy MCDM to Map Risks in Rope Access Work
detail.abstract: Industrial rope access is a work-at-height technique designed to safely reach and operate in elevated areas using ropes and associated equipment. Although regarded as a reliable system, this profession inherently involves significant risks. This study aims to conduct a detailed analysis of these risks and to identify the most effective protective measures. The HRNS method was employed for risk assessment, and the resulting data were statistically analyzed using IBM SPSS. Furthermore, based on expert evaluations, the Fuzzy CRITIC method was applied for criterion weighting, while the Fuzzy TOPSIS method was utilized to determine the most appropriate control measures. The HRNS analysis identified “Employer Responsibilities” and “Environmental Risk Factors” as the most hazardous categories. In contrast, the multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods, offering more precise analytical capabilities, determined that “Environmental Risk Factors” represented the highest level of danger. Additionally, the findings indicated that addressing training deficiencies is the most effective strategy for reducing risks. In conclusion, considering weather conditions in work planning, ensuring personnel certification, providing regular in-house training and drills, addressing educational deficiencies, fulfilling employer obligations, and establishing an Emergency Action Plan (EAP) to support the psychosocial well-being of workers are essential measures for minimizing unacceptable risks in rope access operations.
